questions.stem: Which coast of India receives the majority of its annual rainfall during the retreating northeast monsoon season (October–December)?

options.text: Konkan Coast (Maharashtra–Goa)
Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu)
Malabar Coast (Kerala)
Saurashtra Coast (Gujarat)

questions.explanation: The Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu and southeastern Andhra Pradesh is unique in receiving the bulk of its annual rainfall (about 60%) during the northeast monsoon (October–December), when moisture-laden winds from the Bay of Bengal blow onshore. The Malabar and Konkan coasts receive heavy rainfall during the southwest monsoon (June–September). This puts Tamil Nadu's rainy season out of phase with the rest of India.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has its headquarters at:

options.text: New Delhi
Mumbai
Pune
Kolkata

questions.explanation: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) was established in 1875 and has its main headquarters at Pune (Maharashtra). IMD issues weather forecasts, monsoon predictions, and cyclone warnings for India. It also operates the National Weather Forecasting Centre (NWFC) in New Delhi, but the principal headquarters and research base is in Pune.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The 'Loo' is a characteristic meteorological phenomenon best described as:

options.text: Hot, dry, dusty winds that blow across North Indian plains during May–June afternoons
Heavy pre-monsoon showers along the Kerala coast in April
Cold northerly winds that sweep Rajasthan during December
Violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms in the Bengal delta region

questions.explanation: Loo is a strong, hot, dry, and often dust-laden westerly wind that blows over North Indian plains (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, UP) during May–June afternoons. Temperatures can exceed 45–48°C. It forms due to intense surface heating over the Thar Desert and is responsible for heat waves and deaths. Option D describes Kalbaisakhi (Nor'westers); option B describes Mango showers.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Mawsynram (and nearby Cherrapunji) in Meghalaya receives some of the highest rainfall in the world because of:

options.text: Low-pressure systems from the Bay of Bengal funnelling moisture inland through flat terrain
Western disturbances that redirect Arabian Sea moisture into the Brahmaputra valley
Cyclonic winds rotating from the Arabian Sea that enter Assam through the Brahmaputra gap
The Khasi Hills creating a perfect orographic trap for Bay of Bengal branch moisture, forcing it to rise sharply and release heavy precipitation

questions.explanation: Mawsynram (annual average ~11,872 mm) and Cherrapunji (~11,430 mm) receive extreme rainfall due to orographic lift: the Bay of Bengal branch of the southwest monsoon moves through the funnel-shaped Bengal delta, then strikes the near-vertical southern face of the Khasi Hills (Meghalaya), forcing rapid ascent and condensation. The geographic configuration amplifies rainfall far beyond that of any flat-terrain location.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which phenomenon, originating over the Mediterranean Sea region, brings valuable winter rainfall to the northwestern parts of India?

options.text: Western Disturbances
Nor'westers (Kalbaisakhi)
Southwesterly jet stream migration
ITCZ northward shift

questions.explanation: Western Disturbances are extra-tropical cyclonic disturbances that originate in the Mediterranean Sea and travel eastward along the sub-tropical jet stream. They bring winter precipitation (rain and snowfall) to Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, western Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, and Jammu & Kashmir (November–February). This moisture is critical for Rabi (winter) crops like wheat. Kalbaisakhi are pre-monsoon thunderstorms of Bengal.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: 'Mango showers', which assist mango ripening before the monsoon, occur primarily in:

options.text: Rajasthan during April
Uttar Pradesh during June
Kerala and Karnataka during the pre-monsoon period (April–May)
Tamil Nadu during the northeast monsoon (October–November)

questions.explanation: Mango showers (also called 'pre-monsoon showers') are convective rainfall events that occur over Kerala and Karnataka during April–May before the main southwest monsoon onset. They are driven by intense surface heating and incoming moisture from the Arabian Sea. These showers benefit the mango crop at the ripening stage. Karnataka also has 'Cherry Blossom showers' (coffee blossom rains) that help coffee plants flower.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The southwest monsoon normally arrives at the Kerala coast (officially declared by IMD) around:

options.text: April 15 (±7 days)
June 1 (±7 days)
July 1 (±7 days)
May 15 (±7 days)

questions.explanation: The normal date for the onset of the southwest monsoon over Kerala (the 'burst' of the monsoon) is June 1 (with a standard deviation of about ±7 days). This is when IMD officially declares the monsoon onset, based on criteria including rainfall amounts, wind strength and direction, and cloud cover. From Kerala it advances northward to cover the entire country by mid-July. The monsoon's arrival is a major national weather event.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The Arabian Sea branch of the southwest monsoon, upon striking the Western Ghats, produces an asymmetric rainfall pattern because:

options.text: The windward (western) slopes receive very heavy orographic rainfall while the leeward (eastern) Deccan Plateau falls in a rain shadow and receives far less
The leeward (eastern) slopes receive more rainfall as the moist air descends and cools further
Both sides receive equal rainfall because the Ghats channel moisture evenly through passes
The Ghats deflect all moisture northward, so neither side receives significant rainfall

questions.explanation: Orographic (relief) rainfall occurs when moist air is forced to rise over the Western Ghats. The windward western slopes (Malabar Coast, Konkan) receive 2,500–4,000+ mm annually. As air descends the leeward eastern slopes, it warms and dries (adiabatic warming), creating a rain shadow. Cities like Bengaluru (~900 mm), Pune (~720 mm), and the Deccan interior receive significantly less rainfall than the Ghats western face.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Kalbaisakhi (Nor'westers) are pre-monsoon thunderstorms characterised by violent squalls, hail, and lightning. They particularly affect:

options.text: Punjab and Haryana in April
Kerala and Goa in May
West Bengal and Assam in April–May
Rajasthan in June during the early monsoon

questions.explanation: Kalbaisakhi ('disaster of Baisakh' in Bengali) are violent pre-monsoon squalls that strike West Bengal and parts of Assam in April–May. They occur in the late afternoon and evening when hot, dry air from the northwest meets moist Bay of Bengal air. They can cause damage but also bring relief from summer heat and help pre-monsoon agriculture. Tea gardens in Assam benefit from these 'Bordoichila' (Assamese name for the same phenomenon).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) plays a critical role in Indian monsoon dynamics. Its relevant movement during the Northern Hemisphere summer is:

options.text: Southward into the Southern Indian Ocean, creating a low-pressure pull that drags winds toward Australia
Westward across the Arabian Sea, redirecting monsoon winds toward East Africa
In a circle around the Himalayan axis, creating a vortex effect
Northward over the Indian subcontinent, which establishes a strong low-pressure system that draws in the moisture-laden southwest monsoon

questions.explanation: In summer, the sun's apparent movement north of the equator heats the Indian landmass intensely. The ITCZ (the equatorial trough of low pressure) migrates northward to approximately 20–25°N over India. This creates a steep pressure gradient between the high-pressure Southern Indian Ocean and the low-pressure Indian landmass, which drives the southwest monsoon (actually a modified southeast trade wind that crosses the equator and deflects right due to the Coriolis effect).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: El Niño conditions (warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific) are statistically associated with Indian monsoon rainfall that is:

options.text: Below normal — because El Niño suppresses convective activity over the Indian Ocean and weakens the monsoon pressure gradient
Above normal — because El Niño pumps extra moisture into the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon
Unchanged — Pacific Sea Surface Temperatures have no demonstrated influence on the Indian Ocean monsoon
Concentrated only in the northeast states while the rest of India remains dry

questions.explanation: El Niño events significantly increase the risk of a weak or deficient Indian monsoon. The mechanism involves warming of the central/eastern Pacific → enhanced convection over the Pacific → subsidence and drying over the Indian Ocean → weakened pressure gradient that drives the monsoon. India's worst droughts (1877, 1899, 1972, 1987, 2002, 2009) have often coincided with El Niño years, though the relationship is not deterministic.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which district of India is considered its driest, recording annual rainfall often as low as 100–200 mm?

options.text: Barmer, Rajasthan
Jaisalmer, Rajasthan
Leh, Ladakh
Kachchh, Gujarat

questions.explanation: Jaisalmer district in western Rajasthan, located deep in the Thar Desert, is generally cited as one of the driest places in India with average annual rainfall of about 100–200 mm. It lies far in the interior and is shielded from both the Arabian Sea branch (blocked by the Aravalli range running the wrong direction) and the Bay of Bengal branch (which loses moisture before reaching this far west). Leh is also very dry (~100 mm) but lies in Ladakh, a separate administrative context.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Tamil Nadu receives most of its annual rainfall during October–December because:

options.text: The Arabian Sea branch rebounds off the Western Ghats and redirects onto Tamil Nadu from the west
Western disturbances from the northwest redirect their moisture southward over Tamil Nadu in October
The ITCZ shifts south in October, activating onshore Arabian Sea winds specifically over Tamil Nadu
The northeast (retreating) monsoon winds blow from the northeast, picking up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and making landfall along the Coromandel Coast

questions.explanation: When the southwest monsoon retreats northwestward (from September), northeast trade winds begin to dominate over the Bay of Bengal. These winds pick up moisture as they pass over the warm Bay of Bengal and make landfall on the Coromandel Coast (Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra Pradesh). This northeast monsoon (October–December) is Tamil Nadu's primary rainy season. No other mainland state depends as heavily on this season.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: In the context of Indian monsoon climatology, 'monsoon break' refers to:

options.text: The abrupt onset of the monsoon over Kerala on June 1
The withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from northwest India beginning in mid-September
A temporary cessation or marked weakening of monsoon rainfall over most of India, especially the plains, during an otherwise active monsoon season
The gap between the arrival of the Bay of Bengal branch and the Arabian Sea branch

questions.explanation: A 'monsoon break' is a period during the active monsoon season (July–August) when the monsoon trough (ITCZ) shifts northward to lie along the Himalayan foothills. During this break, rainfall over the plains and peninsula weakens or stops, while the Himalayas and northeast India receive heavy rain. Breaks typically last 5–15 days and are a normal feature of the Indian monsoon rhythm, not the same as monsoon withdrawal.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The concept of a 'rain shadow' in Indian geography directly explains the comparatively low annual rainfall of which region?

options.text: The Malabar Coast (Kerala)
The Andaman Islands
The Shillong Plateau
The Deccan Plateau east of the Western Ghats

questions.explanation: The Western Ghats force the southwest monsoon's Arabian Sea branch to rise and release most of its moisture on the windward western slopes. As air descends the leeward eastern side it warms and dries, leaving the Deccan Plateau in a rain shadow. Interior Deccan cities like Pune (~720 mm) and Bengaluru (~890 mm) receive a fraction of the 3,000–4,000 mm that falls on the Ghats' western face. The Malabar and Andaman coasts are on windward sides and receive heavy rain.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: 'Cherry Blossom rains' or 'coffee blossom rains' are localised pre-monsoon showers that assist coffee flowering and are characteristic of:

options.text: Coorg and other parts of Karnataka
Assam tea gardens
The Nilgiri Hills in Tamil Nadu
Wayanad in Kerala only

questions.explanation: Coffee blossom rains (sometimes called 'cherry blossom rains') occur in the coffee-growing districts of Karnataka — primarily Coorg (Kodagu), Chikkamagaluru, and Hassan — during March–April before the southwest monsoon onset. These isolated convective showers trigger simultaneous flowering (blossom) of coffee plants. The timing and intensity of these rains critically determines the year's coffee yield.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: During the retreating southwest monsoon season (October–November), low-pressure systems forming over the Bay of Bengal frequently intensify into tropical cyclones. These most commonly make landfall along:

options.text: The Gujarat and Maharashtra coasts
The Goa and Karnataka coasts
The Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu coasts
The West Bengal coast only

questions.explanation: October and November are peak months for Bay of Bengal cyclones. During this period warm SSTs (sea surface temperatures) prevail and wind shear is low, enabling cyclone intensification. These cyclones typically track westward and make landfall along the Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu coasts (Coromandel Coast). Tamil Nadu (e.g., Chennai area) and Andhra Pradesh have historically been most cyclone-prone in this season. Odisha is more affected by May and October storms.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The season officially classified by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) as the 'Cold Weather Season' spans:

options.text: October to November
December to February
November to January
January to March

questions.explanation: IMD recognises four meteorological seasons for India: (1) Winter/Cold Weather Season — December to February; (2) Hot/Dry Weather Season — March to May; (3) Southwest Monsoon Season — June to September; (4) Retreating/Northeast Monsoon Season — October to November. December–February sees lowest temperatures, northeast trade winds, and Western Disturbance activity in the northwest.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of India's total annual rainfall is contributed by the southwest monsoon (June–September)?

options.text: About 40%
About 55%
About 75–80%
Over 90%

questions.explanation: The southwest monsoon contributes approximately 75–80% of India's total annual rainfall in just four months (June–September), making it the lifeline of Indian agriculture, water resources, and the economy. This high concentration of rainfall in a short period explains both the intensity of flooding and the severity of droughts when the monsoon is deficient. The remaining 20–25% comes from the northeast monsoon (mainly Tamil Nadu), Western Disturbances (northwest India), and local convective activity.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The Bay of Bengal branch of the southwest monsoon is the first branch to reach India. It initially makes landfall over:

options.text: West Bengal and Odisha simultaneously, splitting between them
The Coromandel Coast of Tamil Nadu from the east
The Gujarat coast after traversing the Arabian Sea
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands, then moves to the northeast before branching westward across the subcontinent

questions.explanation: The Bay of Bengal branch is the first to arrive. It reaches the Andaman and Nicobar Islands around late May (roughly May 20), then hits the northeastern states (Assam, Meghalaya, West Bengal) in early June. From there it splits: one part moves northeastward into the Brahmaputra valley; another moves westward along the Gangetic plains. The Arabian Sea branch hits the Kerala coast around June 1 independently.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: A meteorologist notes that Rajasthan's Thar Desert experiences extreme temperature ranges — near 50°C in summer and near-freezing in winter — far greater than coastal regions at the same latitude. This extreme continentality is primarily caused by:

options.text: High altitude and thin air over the desert plateau that amplifies solar radiation
The desert's great distance from any ocean, its low humidity (poor heat retention), sparse vegetation, and lack of moderating maritime influence
A permanent clockwise wind circulation that traps hot air in summer and cold air in winter
The Aravalli Range blocking all moisture from both coasts and also blocking moderating sea breezes

questions.explanation: Continentality refers to the extreme temperature range experienced by areas far from large water bodies. The Thar Desert's great inland distance means: (a) dry air with low specific heat absorbs and releases heat rapidly; (b) clear skies allow maximum daytime insolation and maximum nocturnal radiation; (c) sandy soil has low heat capacity; (d) no maritime air masses to moderate extremes. The sea breeze effect of the Arabian Sea is blocked by distance and the Aravalli Range.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: La Niña conditions (cooler-than-normal sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific) are generally associated with Indian monsoon rainfall that is:

options.text: Above normal — La Niña strengthens the Walker Circulation, enhancing the pressure gradient and moisture convergence over the Indian Ocean
Below normal — cooler Pacific SSTs divert the monsoon trajectory southward away from India
Unchanged — La Niña operates too far east to influence Indian Ocean dynamics
Concentrated only in northeastern India, leaving central and western India dry

questions.explanation: La Niña (opposite of El Niño) involves cooler-than-normal eastern Pacific SSTs. This strengthens the Walker Circulation (trade winds blow stronger toward the warm western Pacific/Indian Ocean), enhancing deep convection and moisture convergence over the Indian Ocean. The result is typically above-normal Indian monsoon rainfall. Many of India's best monsoon years (e.g., 2020) have coincided with La Niña conditions, though the relationship remains probabilistic.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The thermal low (heat low) over the Thar Desert and Baluchistan plateau during summer is significant for Indian monsoon dynamics because:

options.text: It generates direct orographic rainfall over the Indus-Gangetic plain as air rises over it
It produces northeasterly counter-winds that slow the monsoon advance

It creates an intense low-pressure centre over the landmass that steepens the pressure gradient between the Indian Ocean high-pressure belt and the continent, drawing the moisture-laden southwest monsoon onshore
It is actually a thermal high (anticyclone) — not a low — and deflects the monsoon eastward toward Bangladesh

questions.explanation: By May–June the Thar Desert heats to 45–50°C, generating one of the most intense continental thermal lows in the world. This creates a steep pressure gradient between the Southern Indian Ocean subtropical high (~1020 hPa) and the Thar low (~994 hPa). The large pressure difference drives the Southeast Trade Winds across the equator; they deflect right (Coriolis effect) to become the southwest monsoon. Without this heat low, the driving force of the Indian monsoon would be greatly weakened.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: A student claims: 'Western Ghats receive less total annual rainfall than Mawsynram despite being much closer to the Arabian Sea moisture source.' Which response is correct?

options.text: True — Mawsynram's extreme orographic lift from the Khasi Hills creates more concentrated rainfall than the gentler Ghats slopes despite the longer moisture journey

False — the Western Ghats do receive very heavy rainfall (3,000–4,000+ mm), but Mawsynram's record values result from a different moisture source: the Bay of Bengal branch funnelled and forced up the near-vertical Khasi Hills, not from the same Arabian Sea branch that feeds the Ghats
True — the Arabian Sea branch is weaker than the Bay of Bengal branch, so all inland Meghalaya sites naturally receive more rain than the coast
False — the Western Ghats consistently receive more total rainfall than Mawsynram because their orographic barrier is longer and wider

questions.explanation: The comparison involves two different branches: The Ghats receive the Arabian Sea branch (3,000–4,000+ mm, occasionally more at specific peaks like Agumbe). Mawsynram receives the Bay of Bengal branch, which after entering the funnel-shaped Brahmaputra-Bengal delta strikes the steep, near-vertical Khasi Hills, rising 1,500 m in a very short horizontal distance and releasing extreme precipitation (~11,872 mm). Different branches, different orographic configurations — not a simple distance argument.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Tamil Nadu's rainfall pattern is INCORRECT?

options.text: Tamil Nadu receives the majority of its annual rainfall during the northeast monsoon (October–December)
The northeast monsoon brings moisture-laden winds that blow from the northeast, picking up moisture over the Bay of Bengal before striking the Coromandel Coast
Tamil Nadu's main rainy season is out of phase with most of the rest of peninsular India's southwest monsoon season
Tamil Nadu also receives very heavy southwest monsoon rainfall because its eastern coast is on the windward side of the Western Ghats

questions.explanation: Option D is INCORRECT. Tamil Nadu's eastern coast is on the leeward (rain shadow) side of the Western Ghats with respect to the southwest monsoon. The SW monsoon loses most of its moisture on the windward western slopes. As a result, Tamil Nadu receives comparatively little rainfall during the southwest monsoon season (June–September). Its main rainy season is the northeast monsoon (October–December) — the exact opposite pattern from states on the western coast.
questions.subject: Geography
